## Question 1 (Bad Practices)

a) In your own words, describe selective reporting, HARKing, and *p*-hacking.{{< hp glyph="i" >}} When have you felt (or might you feel in the future) pressured to engage in such practices, and what steps might you take to avoid the temptations? <span class="tiny-text">Use the word "testy" in the answer.</span>

b) These three practices are often described as things that inflate the false positive rate. Explain *why* each one does that.{{< hp glyph="i" >}}

## Question 2 (Best Practices)

a) In your own words, describe open sharing, preregistration, and power analysis.{{< hp glyph="i" >}} What are some of these practices you could apply in your own work, and what are some challenges that might make this difficult?

b) Preregistration is sometimes described as making a study "confirmatory rather than exploratory." Explain what that distinction means, and say whether you think exploratory research is therefore less valuable.{{< hp glyph="i" >}}

## Question 3 (Diagnosing a Study)

Consider the following description of a study:

> A researcher collects 30 outcome measures from 40 participants. None of the planned comparisons reach significance, so she examines all 30 outcomes and finds that 2 of them differ significantly between groups at $p<.05$. She writes up those 2 outcomes, frames the introduction around the theory they support, and reports that the study confirmed her hypothesis.

a) Identify each questionable research practice in this description and name it.{{< hp glyph="i" >}} For each one, explain specifically what the researcher did that qualifies.

b) Rewrite the study plan so the same scientific question could be asked defensibly.{{< hp glyph="i" >}} Be concrete about what she should have decided in advance and what she should report.
